pos: n. (Johann Heinrich Alsted, 1588–1638, professor at Herborn and Weissenburg)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; German Heinrich, ruler of the house; Alsted, from a Westphalian place-name.
biblical_def: Johann Heinrich Alsted set out to put all human learning into one ordered body and very nearly did it. His encyclopaedia of 1630 runs to some seven volumes and takes in logic, metaphysics, mathematics, physics, medicine, law, history and theology, each discipline reduced to definitions, divisions and rules a student could hold. He taught at Herborn, where John Amos Comenius sat under him, and when the war reached the Rhineland he went east to Transylvania and taught at Weissenburg until he died. He was also a convinced chiliast, and published a calculation that the thousand years of Revelation would begin in 1694. The learning was prodigious and the arithmetic was wrong, and both belong in the account. Everything he catalogued had one centre, which is what the apostle says of all things that exist: by him all things consist (Col 1:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines encyclopedia as the circle of sciences, and consist as to stand firm, to subsist, to be supported.
webster_full: ENCYCLOPE'DIA, n. The circle of sciences; a general system of instruction or knowledge.
CONSIST', v.i. To stand together; to be in a fixed or permanent state, as a body composed of parts in union or connection.
DIVIS'ION, n. The act of dividing or separating into parts; the state of being divided; that which divides.
CHIL'IAD, n. A thousand; a collection or sum containing a thousand individuals or particulars.
scriptures: Col 1:17
And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.
Col 2:3
In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
Pro 1:7
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
Act 1:7
And he said unto them, It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power.
corruption_summary: Seven volumes of all knowledge, and one date in Revelation he should not have fixed.
corruption_paragraphs: Alsted's error is instructive and the dictionary names it. He took the thousand years of Revelation and assigned them a calendar date, and the date passed as every such date has passed. The impulse was not idle curiosity but a wish to encourage the Reformed churches in a terrible war; the method was still forbidden. Our Lord shut the question before it was asked: “It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power” (Act 1:7).

The principle to recover is that an ordered mind is a good gift and an unordered boundary is a snare. Knowledge begins where Proverbs puts its beginning, and not where the catalogue begins: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction” (Pro 1:7). All the learning Alsted gathered has one storehouse and one owner: “In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col 2:3).

pos: n. (Wilhelm Zepper, 1550–1607, professor at Herborn and writer on church order)
etymology: German Wilhelm, will-helmet, resolute protector; Zepper, a German family name.
biblical_def: Wilhelm Zepper taught at Herborn and wrote the Reformed church-order book that the German Reformed territories used. His subject was the unglamorous one: how a congregation is governed, who may be ordained, what discipline looks like when it is exercised by elders rather than by a bishop's court, how the catechizing of children is actually to be carried out week by week. He also wrote on preaching and on the duties of the ministry, and his works were reprinted for decades because pastors needed them. The dictionary gives polity a full entry of its own; Zepper is here because somebody has to write the manual. Paul left Titus in Crete with two commissions, to set in order the things that are wanting and to ordain elders in every city (Tit 1:5), and the second is impossible without somebody doing the patient work of the first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines polity as the form of civil or ecclesiastical government, and discipline as instruction and government.
webster_full: POL'ITY, n. The form or constitution of civil government; also, the constitution or governing principles of an ecclesiastical body.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. Instruction and government, comprehending the communication of knowledge and the regulation of practice.
ORDA'IN, v.t. To set apart for an office; to appoint; to invest with ministerial functions or sacerdotal power.
OR'DER, n. Regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things; a regular series or succession.
scriptures: Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Let all things be done decently and in order.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: The man who wrote the manual: ordination, discipline and catechizing, week by week.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the contemporary impatience with church order, which treats polity as a human overlay on a spiritual reality and therefore adjustable at will. Zepper's answer is simply to open the Pastoral Epistles. The apostle does not leave the shape of a congregation to local taste; he leaves instructions, and he treats a disordered church as a church with something wanting.

The principle to recover is that order is commanded and is a mercy to the flock. “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). The eldership exists for a charge it did not invent: “to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28). And discipline has an appointed last court on earth, not a private one: “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17).

“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — reprinted for decades because pastors needed it.
“tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17) — discipline by elders, not by a bishop's court.

pos: n. (Ludwig Crocius, 1586–1655, Bremen theologian and delegate to the Synod of Dort)
etymology: German Ludwig, famous warrior; Latinized Crocius from the German surname Krokisius.
biblical_def: Ludwig Crocius went to Dort as one of the three delegates of the free city of Bremen, and the Bremen delegation is remembered for the mildest voice in that assembly. With Matthias Martinius he pressed the synod to state the gospel's universal call as broadly as the texts permit, and to leave room for the preacher who must say to every hearer that Christ is offered to him. The Canons as adopted do say this, and say it carefully. Crocius spent the rest of his life teaching at Bremen's gymnasium and writing on theology and ethics. The dictionary notes him because a synod needs men who will press the pastoral question, and because the Canons are better for having been examined by a brother who agreed on the substance and worried about the wording. Paul's own word for the office is ambassador, and the embassy is universal in its address (2Co 5:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ambassador as a minister sent as a representative, and offer as to present for acceptance or rejection.
webster_full: AMBAS'SADOR, n. A minister of the highest rank, employed by one prince or state at the court of another, to manage the public concerns of his own.
OF'FER, v.t. To present for acceptance or rejection; to exhibit something that may be taken or received or not.
DEL'EGATE, n. A person appointed and sent by another with powers to transact business as his representative.
ADDRESS', n. A formal application to any one by words or writing; a petition; a speech directed to a person.
scriptures: Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God.
And now, brethren, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up, and to give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: The mildest voice at Dort, and the Canons are the better for it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern reading of Dort as a gathering of hard men who narrowed the gospel, which is the opposite of what the record shows. The Canons state the particular purpose of the atonement and in the same breath command that the gospel be preached without distinction to all who hear. Crocius was one of the men who made sure the second half was not left implied.

The principle to recover is that definite redemption and an unrestricted offer are both Scripture's, and a preacher who drops either has stopped quoting. “Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God” (2Co 5:20). And the flock is committed to a word that does the work: “I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up” (Act 20:32).

“the word of his grace, which is able to build you up” (Act 20:32) — a brother who worried about the wording.
“which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — the substance never in doubt.

pos: n. (Hermann Ravensperger, 1586–1625, professor at Steinfurt and Groningen)
etymology: German Hermann, army-man, warrior; Ravensperger, from a Westphalian place-name.
biblical_def: Hermann Ravensperger taught theology at the Reformed academy of Steinfurt in Westphalia and then, from its founding years, at the new university of Groningen, where he was among the first professors of divinity. He died at thirty-nine, having spent his working life in the two kinds of institution the Reformed built wherever they could: the small territorial academy that trained a county's pastors, and the new northern university that would train a province's. Neither was grand. Both were a deliberate answer to the simple fact that a Reformed church without a school becomes a Reformed church without ministers in twenty-five years. The apostolic pattern is a chain of four links in one verse, and the third link is a schoolroom of some kind: faithful men who shall be able to teach others also (2Ti 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines academy as a school of the higher kind, and professor as one who publicly teaches a science.
webster_full: ACAD'EMY, n. A school, or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university or college and a common school.
PRO'FESSOR, n. One that publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; particularly, an officer in a university.
SEM'INARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university, in which persons are instructed.
SUCCES'SION, n. A following of things in order; a series of things following one another in time or place.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
corruption_summary: A county academy and a new northern university, and thirty-nine years to serve them in.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a church can live on preaching alone and leave the training of preachers to providence. The Reformed did not believe it and acted accordingly: wherever a territory went over, a school followed within a generation, because the alternative was a pulpit filled by whoever happened to be available.

The principle to recover is that the ministry is a succession, and a succession must be taught. “And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). The psalmist states the same obligation as a refusal: “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4).

roots_lines: Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to commit, to entrust as a deposit; 2 Timothy 2:2.
Greek hikanos (G2425) — sufficient, competent, able; 2 Timothy 2:2.
Hebrew saphar (H5608) — to recount, to rehearse, to declare; Psalm 78:4.
Hebrew kachad (H3582) — to hide, to conceal, to withhold; Psalm 78:4.
Hebrew daath (H1847) — knowledge, perception; Malachi 2:7.
usage: “the same commit thou to faithful men” (2Ti 2:2) — Steinfurt, then the new Groningen.
“We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4) — a school within a generation, or no ministers.
“it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2) — dead at thirty-nine.

pos: n. (Conrad Bergius, 1592–1642, Reformed preacher at Bremen)
etymology: German Konrad, bold counsel; Latinized Bergius from the German surname Berg.
biblical_def: Conrad Bergius preached at Bremen in the worst years of the Thirty Years War, and he belonged to a family that gave the Reformed cause two notable brothers: Conrad in the free city, and Johann as court preacher at Berlin, whose whole labour was to get Lutherans and Reformed to live in one Brandenburg without destroying each other. Conrad shared the irenic temper and kept the Reformed substance, which is a harder combination than either half alone. The dictionary is careful here. Peace between confessions that genuinely agree on the gospel is a duty; peace purchased by leaving the gospel undefined is not peace at all, and Paul puts the limit in the sharpest possible form in his letter to the Galatians (Gal 1:8). Bergius stood inside the limit, and the pleasantness of brethren dwelling together is a real blessing when the brethren actually hold the same faith (Psa 133:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines irenic as pacific and conciliatory, and union as the junction of two or more things.
webster_full: IREN'IC, a. Pacific; tending to promote peace; of or pertaining to peace.
U'NION, n. The act of joining two or more things into one, and thus forming a compound body; concord; agreement.
AC'CURSED, pp. Doomed to destruction or misery; separated from the favor of God.
CON'CORD, n. Agreement between persons; union in opinions, sentiments, views or interests.
scriptures: A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
corruption_summary: Irenic in temper and Reformed in substance, in a city at war for thirty years.
corruption_paragraphs: A real danger attends this kind of ministry and the dictionary names it. Irenicism that begins by seeking agreement among brethren can end by treating the points of disagreement as unimportant, and the seventeenth century produced men who travelled that whole road. The test is whether the gospel itself is left defined. Paul fixes the boundary with no allowance for temperament at all: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8).

The principle to recover is that peace and truth are not rivals but are ordered, truth first. “For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints” (1Co 14:33). And the direction of search is backward to what was given, not forward to what can be agreed: “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls” (Jer 6:16).

Hebrew nethibah (H5410) — a path, a way trodden out; Jeremiah 6:16.

“let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8) — the boundary no temperament may move.
“ask for the old paths, where is the good way” (Jer 6:16) — irenic in temper, Reformed in substance.

pos: n. (Georg Pasor, 1570–1637, Greek lexicographer of Herborn and Franeker)
etymology: Greek Georgios, a husbandman; Latin pastor, a shepherd, whence the surname Pasor.
biblical_def: Georg Pasor wrote the dictionary of New Testament Greek that generations of Reformed students actually used. Published in 1619 and reprinted for a century and a half, it did something no earlier lexicon had done so thoroughly: it confined itself to the vocabulary of the Greek New Testament, gave every word its senses with the places where each sense occurs, and so put into a student's hands the means of reading the text rather than reading about it. He taught at Herborn and ended at Franeker in Friesland. The work is the sort nobody praises and everybody uses, and it is the reason a country pastor in 1700 could check his preaching against the Greek. Jeremiah describes what such a book is for, and the eating is the point: thy words were found, and I did eat them (Jer 15:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lexicon as a dictionary or vocabulary, and philology as the study of language and literature.
webster_full: LEX'ICON, n. A dictionary; a vocabulary or book containing an alphabetical arrangement of the words in a language, with the definition of each.
PHILOL'OGY, n. Primarily, a love of words, or a desire to know the origin and construction of language.
VOCAB'ULARY, n. A list or collection of the words of a language, arranged in alphabetical order and explained.
SENSE, n. Meaning; import; signification; as the true sense of words or phrases.
scriptures: Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart: for I am called by thy name, O LORD God of hosts.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Pro 30:5
Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: A New Testament lexicon reprinted for a century and a half, and used by men nobody remembers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the suspicion that attention to the original languages is a scholar's indulgence that gets between a believer and his Bible. Pasor's lexicon was built for the opposite purpose. Its whole design is to shorten the distance: a man who can look up a word for himself is no longer dependent on another man's report of what the word means.

The principle to recover is that every word of the text is given and therefore every word repays the labour. “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2Ti 3:16). The purity is at the level of the word itself: “Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him” (Pro 30:5). And the aim of all such apparatus is Nehemiah's: “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8).

roots_lines: Greek theopneustos (G2315) — God-breathed, inspired of God; 2 Timothy 3:16.
Greek ophelimos (G5624) — profitable, useful, helpful; 2 Timothy 3:16.

Hebrew akal (H398) — to eat, to consume, to take in; Jeremiah 15:16.
Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to refine, to try, to purify; Proverbs 30:5.

“All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) — and therefore every word repays the labour.
“gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — Herborn, and then Franeker.

pos: n. (Caspar Sibelius, 1590–1658, Reformed minister of Deventer)
etymology: Persian Gaspar, treasurer, through Latin Caspar; Latinized Sibelius from the Dutch surname Sibel.
biblical_def: Caspar Sibelius served the church at Deventer in the Dutch province of Overijssel for most of his working life, preached through long stretches of Scripture, and left an autobiography that tells the ordinary truth about a seventeenth-century Reformed ministry: the wars that came past the town, the plague years, the quarrels in the consistory, the deaths of his children, the sermons that had to be preached on the following Sunday regardless. He also took a real interest in the Dutch mission work in Formosa and the East, and his writings on it are among the earliest Reformed missionary accounts. He is in the dictionary as the measure of the pastorate: not a controversy and not a system, but one congregation kept for forty years. The charge is stated once and covers the whole of it: feed the flock of God which is among you (1Pe 5:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pastor as a minister having charge of a church, and oversight as watchful care and superintendence.
webster_full: PAS'TOR, n. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation, whose duty is to watch over the people of his charge.
O'VERSIGHT, n. Superintendence; watchful care; as the oversight of a church.
FLOCK, n. A company or collection; applied to sheep and other small animals; the congregation of a church.
JOUR'NAL, n. A diary; an account of daily transactions and events.
scriptures: Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
corruption_summary: Forty years in one Dutch town: plague, war, consistory quarrels, and a sermon due on Sunday.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern hunger for a ministry that is interesting, which quietly teaches young men that staying is a failure of ambition. Sibelius stayed. The diary he left is not a record of achievement; it is a record of a man turning up, and the congregation at Deventer had the gospel preached to it for four decades because he did.

The principle to recover is that oversight is willing, unmercenary and local. “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). The flock was bought at a price that fixes its worth: “to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28). And the people are told to look at the end of such a life: “whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation” (Heb 13:7).

roots_lines: Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend as a shepherd, to feed and lead; 1 Peter 5:2.
Greek episkopeo (G1983) — to oversee, to exercise the oversight; 1 Peter 5:2.
Greek anagkastos (G317) — by constraint, of necessity; 1 Peter 5:2.
Greek aischrokerdos (G147) — for base gain, greedily; 1 Peter 5:2.
Greek anastrophe (G391) — manner of life, conversation, conduct; Hebrews 13:7.
usage: “Feed the flock of God which is among you” (1Pe 5:2) — Deventer, through plague and war.
“not by constraint, but willingly” (1Pe 5:2) — forty years and a plain diary.
“considering the end of their conversation” (Heb 13:7) — the measure of a pastorate.

pos: n. (Menso Alting, 1541–1612, reformer and chief pastor of Emden)
etymology: Frisian Menso, a given name of the region; Alting, a Frisian family name.
biblical_def: Menso Alting made Emden what the sixteenth century called the mother church of the Dutch Reformation. He came to the East Frisian port in 1575 and served it for thirty-seven years as its leading minister, in the decades when Emden was the refuge of Dutch Protestants driven out by Alva, the place where their first synod met, the press from which their books went home, and the training ground of their ministers. He also led the townsmen in resisting their count's attempt to force a Lutheran settlement, and the city kept its Reformed order. Emden's whole significance is that somebody took the refugees in. Scripture makes that obligation an inference from Israel's own history rather than a sentiment: love ye therefore the stranger (Deu 10:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines refuge as shelter or protection from danger, and stranger as a foreigner, one who is not a native.
webster_full: REF'UGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger.
STRAN'GER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one not an inhabitant of the place.
ASY'LUM, n. A sanctuary or place of refuge, where criminals and debtors found shelter.
SYN'OD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
scriptures: Love ye therefore the stranger: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
corruption_summary: The mother church of the Dutch Reformation was a port that took the refugees in.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the flattening of the biblical stranger into a modern political abstraction, so that the duty is either dissolved into open borders or dismissed as sentiment. Scripture is more specific and more demanding than either. Israel is told to love the stranger because Israel was a stranger, and Emden obeyed the command in the concrete form it took in 1575: houses, work, a church in the exiles' own tongue, and a press.

The principle to recover is that hospitality to the exiled brother is commanded, costly and historically fruitful. “Love ye therefore the stranger: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Deu 10:19). The writer to the Hebrews adds a motive nobody can calculate in advance: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2).

pos: n. (Nicolaus Arnoldi, 1618–1680, professor of theology at Franeker)
etymology: Greek Nikolaos, victor of the people, Latinized Nicolaus; Arnoldi, son of Arnold.
biblical_def: Nicolaus Arnoldi was a Pole who became a Frisian. Born in Lesno in Poland, he came west to study, settled in the Netherlands, and held the chair of theology at Franeker for more than thirty years. His great labour was the refutation of Socinianism, the denial of the Trinity and of the deity of Christ that had taken organized form in his native Poland and was then being pressed on the Dutch churches in print. He answered it at length and in detail, because the Socinians argued from the text and had to be answered from the text. The dictionary records the error by its own name, as it always does. If the Son of God is not God, then Thomas was permitted to worship a creature and was commended for it, and that is the shortest road to the conclusion: my Lord and my God (Joh 20:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Socinianism as the doctrine of Socinus, denying the divinity of Christ, and refute as to disprove.
webster_full: SOCIN'IANISM, n. The doctrines or system of the Socinians, who deny the divinity of Christ and the doctrine of the Trinity.
REFU'TE, v.t. To disprove; to prove to be false or erroneous, either by argument or by countervailing proof.
DEI'TY, n. Godhead; divinity; the nature and essence of the Supreme Being.
HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
scriptures: And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Tit 2:13
Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;

And we know that the Son of God is come, and hath given us an understanding, that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, even in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life.
corruption_summary: A Pole at Franeker, answering the Socinian denial of Christ's deity from the texts it misused.
corruption_paragraphs: Socinianism is named here by its own name. Arising with Lelio and Faustus Socinus in the sixteenth century and taking organized shape in Poland, it denies the Trinity, denies that the Son is God of the same essence with the Father, and consequently denies the substitutionary satisfaction, since a creature cannot bear the wrath of God for other creatures. It is not a variant of Christianity but a different religion using Christian words, and the modern unitarian and much of liberal Protestantism descend from it.

The principle to recover is that the deity of Christ is not inferred from a system but read on the page. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1). Thomas is not rebuked for what he said but answered: “My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28). Paul names one Person with both titles: “the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Tit 2:13). And John closes the matter: “This is the true God, and eternal life” (1Jn 5:20).
roots_summary: Greek theos (G2316), God; Greek logos (G3056), word, utterance, the eternal Word.
roots_lines: Greek logos (G3056) — word, utterance, the eternal Word of God; John 1:1.
Greek theos (G2316) — God, the Deity; John 1:1.
Greek kurios (G2962) — Lord, master, owner; John 20:28.
Greek megas (G3173) — great; of God, the great God; Titus 2:13.
Greek alethinos (G228) — true, genuine, real; 1 John 5:20.
usage: “the Word was God” (Joh 1:1) — thirty years in the Franeker chair.
“My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28) — the shortest road to the conclusion.
“This is the true God, and eternal life” (1Jn 5:20) — the Socinian denial answered at length.

pos: n. (Samuel Desmarets, 1599–1673, professor of theology at Groningen)
etymology: Hebrew Shemuel, heard of God, or asked of God; French Desmarets, Latinized Maresius.
biblical_def: Samuel Maresius was a French Reformed minister who became the most combative theologian in the northern Netherlands. Trained at Saumur and Geneva, he pastored in France, served at Maastricht, and from 1643 held the Groningen chair for thirty years. He fought almost everyone: Rome, the Socinians, the Jesuits, the Labadists who drew a party out of the Dutch churches, the Cartesian theologians who wanted to begin with doubt, and in his last years his own colleagues over how far the new philosophy might be let in. He was not always right and was never quiet. The dictionary neither excuses the temper nor pretends the battles were imaginary, because every one of them concerned whether the Reformed churches would keep a defined gospel. Paul's charge to Titus names the two halves of the office, to exhort and to convince the gainsayers (Tit 1:9), and Maresius was heavily weighted to the second.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines controvertist as one who carries on a controversy, and gainsayer as one who contradicts or opposes.
webster_full: CONTROVER'TIST, n. One who controverts; a disputant; a man versed or engaged in controversy.
GAINSA'YER, n. One who contradicts or denies what is alleged; an opposer.
EXHORT', v.t. To incite by words or advice; to animate or urge to any good conduct or practice.
DOUBT, n. A fluctuation of mind respecting truth or propriety, arising from defect of knowledge or evidence.
scriptures: Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Thirty years at Groningen fighting Rome, the Socinians, the Labadists and the Cartesians.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the Cartesian question since Maresius spent his last strength on it. To begin theology with methodical doubt, as the new philosophy proposed, is to make the human mind the court before which revelation must appear, and the Reformed who resisted it were not obscurantists but were defending the order of knowing: God speaks, and the creature hears. Where Maresius overreached was in temper and in the multiplication of enemies, and that is a real fault in a minister, not a mere eccentricity.

The principle to recover is that controversy is an office, and an office has a rule. “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9). The measure is never the disputant's vigour but the word he holds: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).

Greek epagonizomai (G1864) — to contend earnestly for; Jude 3.

“earnestly contend for the faith” (Jud 1:3) — Rome, the Socinians, the Labadists, the Cartesians.
“if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20) — never quiet, not always right.
